results.summary_before: This power management IC generates two complementary PWM outputs with duty cycles controlled by an external ADC, using a heartbeat signal to periodically initiate ADC conversions and update the PWM. It reads an 8-bit parallel ADC (AD7819) and drives a high-side driver (MCP14700) for a half-bridge configuration, with a built-in dead zone to prevent shoot-through. The design uses state machines to sequence ADC read and PWM update, and is intended for power conversion applications. External hardware includes the specified ADC and high-side driver.
results.summary: This power management IC generates two complementary PWM outputs with duty cycles controlled by an external ADC, using a heartbeat signal to periodically initiate ADC conversions and update the PWM. It reads an 8-bit parallel ADC (AD7819) and drives a high-side driver (MCP14700) for a half-bridge configuration, with a built-in dead zone to prevent shoot-through. The design uses state machines to sequence the ADC read and PWM update so the two outputs remain 180 degrees out of phase. External hardware includes the specified ADC and high-side driver.

results.summary_before: This design implements a 4-bit stochastic multiplier using traditional architecture. It converts two 4-bit binary vectors into stochastic bitstreams using a PRBS and comparator, then multiplies them with an AND gate. External hardware includes an ADLAM2000 for control and analysis. The design is part of a study on stochastic computing.
results.summary: This design implements a 4-bit stochastic multiplier using a traditional architecture. It converts two 4-bit binary-weighted vectors into 1-bit serial stochastic streams using a PRBS and a comparator, then multiplies them with a two-input AND gate. The serial multiplier output and the intermediate stochastic streams and PRBS signals are brought to the outputs for observation. External hardware includes an ADLAM2000 for control and analysis of the stochastic bitstreams.

results.summary_before: This is a baremetal RISC-V RV32E system-on-chip that includes a UART, a QSPI memory controller for PSRAM and flash, a generic SPI interface, and a sigma-delta audio emulator. It is designed to run firmware from external NOR flash and requires a PMOD with flash and PSRAM for operation. The design was tested by the author and successfully ran MicroPython for RV32E and played audio. It is notable for being a compact RISC-V SoC implementation on a Tiny Tapeout tile.

results.summary_before: This design is a linear feedback shift register random number generator that interfaces via a Wishbone bus to fit within the Tiny Tapeout pin constraints. It allows loading a seed through the bus and then outputs a pseudo-random bit stream. Testing requires a cocotb testbench and a microcontroller on the development board to apply the correct startup signals. The design is a compact digital implementation of an LFSR with bus interface.

results.summary_before: This design multiplies two 8-bit signed numbers to produce a 16-bit product using a modified Booth encoding algorithm. The Booth-recoded bits feed a Dadda multiplier tree, and the partial products are summed in a carry-lookahead adder. The multiplicand is applied on the eight input pins while the product is split across the output and bidirectional pins. No external hardware is required, and the design is a straightforward arithmetic accelerator with no reported silicon results.
results.summary: This design multiplies two 8-bit signed numbers to produce a 16-bit product using a modified Booth encoding algorithm. The Booth-recoded bits feed a Dadda multiplier design, and the partial products are added in a carry-lookahead adder. The multiplicand is applied on the eight input pins while the product is split across the output and bidirectional pins. No external hardware is required.

results.summary_before: This design implements a 4-bit Gaussian blur filter that accepts nine pixel values serially through a free-running shift register and outputs the blurred center pixel. After nine clock cycles the shift register is full and the output can be sampled, with the last shift register stage also exposed for testing. The design is written in Wokwi and runs at 100 kHz on a single tile. An FPGA is suggested as useful external hardware for driving the pixel stream, and the documentation is brief but sufficient to understand the operation.
